stem: Ada needs to change a setting of the build daemon that applies to the whole machine. Under which directory are system-wide configuration files kept?

options.rationale: That directory holds log files, which programs write while they run.
That directory shows kernel and process data, made up on the fly.
It holds the machine’s configuration files, mostly as plain text.
That directory holds the kernel and boot loader files.

explanation: System-wide configuration lives in `/etc`, as mostly plain text files that root can edit, for example `/etc/tuxpixel/buildd.conf`. Settings that affect only one user are normally kept in hidden files in that user’s home directory.

stem: Jonas changes a setting of his text editor that should apply only to his account. Where does the program normally keep it?

options.text: In a hidden file or directory whose name starts with a dot, inside his home directory.
options.rationale: Per-user settings stay out of the way of other users.

options.text: In `/etc`, in a file that every user on the machine reads and that only root may edit.
options.rationale: Files in `/etc` apply to the whole machine and are changed by root.

options.text: In `/proc`, where the kernel keeps a settings file for each user account.
options.rationale: `/proc` shows kernel data and is rebuilt while the system runs, so nothing is stored there.

options.text: In `/boot`, next to the kernel, so that the setting is read before any user logs in.
options.rationale: `/boot` holds only start-up files, not the settings of programs.

explanation: System-wide settings are in `/etc`. A setting that belongs to one user is stored in a hidden file (a “dot file”) or a hidden directory in that user’s home directory, such as `~/.config`.

stem: Which of these is a program, as opposed to a configuration file or a log file?

options.rationale: It is a configuration file holding the machine’s name.
It is a configuration file of the build daemon.
It is a log file that records package changes.
It is an executable file on disk that becomes a process when run.

explanation: A program is a file on disk that can be run, such as `/usr/bin/ls`. Configuration files in `/etc` only tell programs how to behave, and log files under `/var/log` record what happened.

stem: What is special about the process with PID 1 on a Linux system?

options.text: It is the process that uses the most memory, so the kernel numbers it first when the machine starts.
options.rationale: PIDs are numbers handed out in order and have nothing to do with memory use.

options.text: It is the first process the kernel starts, and it starts the others, directly or indirectly.
options.rationale: On most distributions it is systemd.

options.text: It is the shell of the first user who logged in, and it ends when they log out.
options.rationale: The shell is an ordinary process with a later PID.

options.text: It is reserved for the kernel’s log messages, and no other program may use it.
options.rationale: PID 1 is a normal process, and the kernel’s ring buffer is read with `dmesg`.

explanation: The kernel starts one first process, PID 1. It starts everything else, so every other process has a parent. On most modern distributions PID 1 is systemd, which also starts and supervises the services.

stem: Ada wants a live view of the processes, redrawn every few seconds and sorted by CPU use. Which command does this?

options.rationale: It prints one snapshot and then exits.
It updates continuously and shows the busiest processes first.
It shows memory use, not processes.
It prints kernel messages from the ring buffer.

explanation: `top` is the live view: it redraws every few seconds, sorted by CPU use by default. `ps` takes a single snapshot, `free` reports memory, and `dmesg` shows kernel messages.

stem: Which command shows every process on the system in the full format, with columns such as UID, PID, PPID and start time?

options.rationale: Without `-e` it lists only the processes of the current terminal.
It shows a single process, the one with PID 1.
Without options it shows only the processes of the current terminal.
`-e` selects every process and `-f` chooses the full format.

explanation: `ps -ef` lists every process in the full format. Plain `ps` or `ps -f` shows only the processes in your current terminal, and `ps -p` picks processes by PID. The BSD-style `ps aux` also lists all processes.

stem: Inside a running `top`, which key sorts the process list by memory use?

options.rationale: It sorts by the share of memory used.
It sorts by CPU use.
It quits top.
It asks for a PID and kills that process.

explanation: In `top`, `M` sorts by memory, `P` sorts by CPU, `k` kills a process and `q` quits. `h` shows the help screen with all keys.

stem: In the output of `ps aux`, a process shows the state `Z` in the STAT column. What does that mean?

options.text: It is running right now on a CPU.
options.rationale: A running process is marked `R`.

options.text: It is sleeping and waits for an event, such as input from the keyboard.
options.rationale: A sleeping process is marked `S`.

options.text: It is a zombie: it has ended, but its parent has not yet collected its exit status.
options.rationale: Zombies use no CPU time and disappear once the parent reads the status.

options.text: It is stopped by a signal until it receives the order to continue.
options.rationale: A stopped process is marked `T`.

explanation: The state letter in the STAT column of `ps` tells what the process is doing: `R` running, `S` sleeping, `T` stopped and `Z` zombie, which is a finished process whose parent has not collected its exit status yet.

stem: The top line of `top` shows `load average: 0.05, 0.10, 0.20`. What do the three numbers mean?

options.text: The share of CPU time used by the first, second and third busiest process.
options.rationale: The load average is a system-wide figure, not a per-process one.

options.text: The memory use of RAM, swap and the disk cache, as shares of the total.
options.rationale: Memory is shown on separate lines of top.

options.text: The number of running, sleeping and zombie processes at this moment.
options.rationale: Those counts are shown on the “Tasks” line.

options.text: The average system load over the last 1, 5 and 15 minutes.
options.rationale: They show how busy the CPU has been recently.

explanation: The load average is the average number of processes that wanted the CPU over the last 1, 5 and 15 minutes. A value near the number of CPU cores means the machine is fully used.

stem: Mira starts `ls` in two different terminals at the same time. How many processes and how many programs are involved?

options.text: One process and one program, because the kernel runs a program only once.
options.rationale: Every run creates a new process, even of the same program.

options.text: Two processes, each with its own PID, and one program, the file `/usr/bin/ls`.
options.rationale: Each running copy of a program is a separate process.

options.text: Two processes and two programs, because each terminal has its own copy of the file.
options.rationale: Both processes run the same program file on disk.

options.text: One process and two programs, because the terminals share one process list.
options.rationale: Each running copy is a process of its own, with its own PID.

explanation: A program is a file on disk. A process is one running instance of it, with its own PID. Running `ls` twice means two processes of the same program.

stem: In the output of `free`, which column best tells how much memory programs can still use without swapping?

options.rationale: It counts only memory that is completely unused, which is usually small because Linux uses spare RAM as cache.
It shows memory in use, not what is left.
It estimates the memory that can be given to programs, including cache that can be freed.
It shows memory shared between processes, mostly temporary file systems.

explanation: A small value in the `free` column is normal, because Linux uses spare RAM as a disk cache and gives it back when programs need it. `available` is the better guide for what programs can still use.

stem: The asset server runs out of RAM during a big build. What is swap, and how does it help?

options.text: It is disk space that the kernel uses as extra memory when RAM is full, but it is much slower than RAM.
options.rationale: Heavy swapping makes a machine feel slow.

options.text: It is a second copy of the RAM that the kernel keeps on disk to make memory access faster and to protect it after a power cut.
options.rationale: Swap isn’t a mirror of RAM, and the disk is slower, not faster.

options.text: It is a cache for the processor that holds the most recent instructions, inside the CPU.
options.rationale: That describes a CPU cache, which is built into the processor.

options.text: It is a partition that stores the kernel and the boot loader files for the next start.
options.rationale: Those files live in `/boot`.

explanation: Swap is disk space (a partition or a file) that the kernel can use as overflow memory when RAM is full. It keeps programs from being killed, but it is far slower than RAM. `free` shows the swap total and use in its last line.

stem: Why can one crashing program not overwrite the memory of another program on Linux?

options.text: The kernel gives each process its own virtual address space, mapped to real memory by the kernel.
options.rationale: A process only sees its own addresses.

options.text: Every program has to be started by root, so no ordinary user can start two at once and cannot be run in parallel.
options.rationale: Programs of ordinary users run at the same time without any special rights.

options.text: All programs share one block of RAM, which the kernel locks as soon as one program is running.
options.rationale: The kernel doesn’t lock memory this way; memory is divided between processes.

options.text: The processor stores each program in swap first, so it can never reach RAM.
options.rationale: Swap is used only when RAM is full, and doesn’t isolate programs.

explanation: Processes don’t see the real memory addresses. The kernel gives each of them its own virtual address space and maps it to physical RAM (or swap). A program can’t even name an address that belongs to another process.

stem: A line in `/proc/1234/maps` begins with `7f3c2a000000-7f3c2a021000`. What are these two numbers?

options.text: Decimal process IDs: the process and the parent that started it and the user that owns both.
options.rationale: Process IDs are small decimal numbers, and `maps` is not a list of them.

options.text: Octal permission modes of the two files that the process has opened.
options.rationale: Permissions look like `rw-` or `644` and don’t form ranges.

options.text: Hexadecimal memory addresses: the start and the end of an area of the process’s memory.
options.rationale: The addresses are virtual ones, valid only inside process 1234.

options.text: IPv6 addresses of the two network connections that the process has made.
options.rationale: IPv6 addresses use colons, and `maps` doesn’t list network connections.

explanation: `/proc/<PID>/maps` lists the memory areas of a process. Each line starts with the start and end address of an area, written in hexadecimal. They are virtual addresses that belong to that process.

stem: Which file shows the total and the free memory of the machine as text that `cat` or `grep` can read?

options.rationale: `/etc` holds configuration files, and no such file exists there.
The kernel builds it when it is read, and `free` uses the same data.
`/var/log` holds logs, not a live memory report.
`/boot` holds start-up files, not live system data.

explanation: `/proc` is a pseudo-filesystem that the kernel makes up on the fly. `/proc/meminfo` reports memory, `/proc/cpuinfo` the processor, and `/proc/<PID>/` one process. `free`, `ps` and `top` read their data from there.

stem: On a systemd machine, Mira wants to stop the running service `buildd` right now. Which command does this?

options.rationale: It only shows the state of the service and doesn’t change it.
It changes what happens at boot, but leaves a running service running.
It makes the service start at boot, and doesn’t stop it.
It stops the service at once and needs root rights.

explanation: `systemctl stop` ends a service immediately, `start` starts it and `status` shows its state. `enable` and `disable` only control whether the service starts at boot.

stem: Mira started `pixel-raiders-server` yesterday, but after a reboot it is not running. Which command makes it start at every boot?

options.rationale: It runs the service now and doesn’t change what happens at the next boot.
It only reports the state of the unit.
`enable` links the unit into the boot sequence.
It ends the service, and it would stay stopped.

explanation: `start` affects only the current run. To start a service at every boot you `enable` it, and `disable` removes that. Both can be combined with `--now` to act at once as well.

stem: Which description fits a service, also called a daemon?

options.text: A process that runs in the background and waits for requests, such as an SSH or build server.
options.rationale: systemd starts and watches most of them.

options.text: A configuration file in `/etc` that tells the kernel which programs may be started.
options.rationale: A service is a running process and not a file of settings.

options.text: A program that runs in the foreground and quits as soon as the user closes the terminal or when the session ends.
options.rationale: Services keep running with no terminal attached.

options.text: A hardware component that has to be plugged in before the system can start programs.
options.rationale: A service is software, started by the system itself.

explanation: A service (daemon) is a background process that waits for work: a web server, an SSH server, a build daemon. On systemd systems, PID 1 starts and supervises services, which are described by unit files such as `ssh.service`.

stem: Mira wants to read only the journal messages of the `ssh` service. Which command does this?

options.rationale: It shows only the messages of the kernel.
It shows all messages since the current boot, from every service.
It follows the journal and prints new messages of every service as they arrive.
`-u` selects one unit.

explanation: `journalctl -u NAME` limits the output to one unit. `-b` limits it to the current boot, `-k` to kernel messages, `-n N` to the last N lines and `-f` follows new messages.

stem: Under which directory do most services write their plain text log files?

options.rationale: The configuration directory has no standard place for logs.
Files such as `syslog`, `auth.log` and `dpkg.log` are there.
`/proc` shows kernel data and doesn’t store logs.
`/boot` holds the kernel and boot loader files.

explanation: Logs are variable data, so they live under `/var`, in `/var/log`. They are plain text, so `less`, `tail` and `grep` work on them. Configuration is in `/etc`.

stem: What is the kernel ring buffer that `dmesg` prints?

options.text: A text file in `/var/log` that the kernel appends to forever until the disk is full.
options.rationale: It is a memory buffer of fixed size, not a file that grows forever.

options.text: A fixed-size area of memory where the kernel stores its messages, and new ones overwrite the oldest.
options.rationale: It records hardware found at boot, drivers and devices plugged in.

options.text: A list of the processes that the kernel has started, kept in `/proc`.
options.rationale: Processes are listed by `ps`, and not in the ring buffer.

options.text: A cache for disk blocks that makes reading files faster and is flushed at every shutdown.
options.rationale: That is the page cache, not the kernel’s message buffer.

explanation: The kernel keeps its own messages (hardware found at boot, driver loading, devices plugged in, disk errors) in a ring buffer of fixed size, where new lines overwrite the oldest. `dmesg` prints it, and `journalctl -k` shows the same messages.

stem: A USB drive disconnected by itself in the middle of a transfer. Which command helps Mira see what the kernel reported about it?

options.rationale: It shows running processes, not kernel messages about devices.
It reports memory and swap and says nothing about devices.
It prints name-to-address pairs for networking.
It prints the newest lines of the kernel ring buffer.

explanation: Kernel messages about hardware, such as a USB port, are in the ring buffer. `dmesg` prints it, and many systems restrict it to root, so the command is run with `sudo`. `tail` limits the output to the newest lines.

stem: In syslog, what is a “facility”?

options.text: A category of the program that sends the message, such as `auth`, `kern`, `mail` or `daemon`.
options.rationale: The facility tells which part of the system the message comes from.

options.text: The level of seriousness of the message, from `debug` up to `emerg` and is stored in the log line.
options.rationale: That is the priority, also called the severity.

options.text: The name of the log file in `/var/log` where the message is finally written.
options.rationale: The configuration maps facilities and priorities to files, but a file is not a facility.

options.text: The host name of the computer that the message was sent to.
options.rationale: A host name is a separate field of a log line.

explanation: Syslog sorts messages by facility (who sent it) and priority (how serious it is). The configuration decides which combinations are written to which files.

stem: Which of these syslog priorities is the most serious one?

options.rationale: It is an error condition, less serious than critical.
It warns about something that may become a problem.
It is a critical condition, more serious than an error.
It is a purely informational message.

explanation: From the most to the least serious, the syslog priorities are `emerg`, `alert`, `crit`, `err`, `warning`, `notice`, `info` and `debug`. Among the options, `crit` is the most serious one.

stem: On a Debian-based machine that uses rsyslog, which file sets which messages are written to which log file?

options.rationale: It is a log file that collects messages; it doesn’t hold the rules.
It controls how old log files are rotated, not what gets logged.
It maps names to addresses and has nothing to do with logging.
Rules there map facilities and priorities to files in `/var/log`.

explanation: The syslog service reads its rules from a configuration file, `/etc/rsyslog.conf` on systems with rsyslog. The rules map facility and priority combinations to log files in `/var/log` or to other places.

stem: Mira wants to check who tried to log in and who used `sudo` on a Debian-based server that uses rsyslog. Which log file records this?

options.rationale: It records which packages were installed or removed.
Authentication events are logged there on Debian-based systems.
It holds messages from the kernel.
It records what the package tool apt did.

explanation: On Debian-based systems, authentication messages such as logins, failed passwords and `sudo` use go to `/var/log/auth.log`. On Enterprise Linux the equivalent is `/var/log/secure`. Some of these files can be read only by root.

stem: What does logrotate do?

options.text: It sorts the lines of each log file by time, so the newest message is at the top.
options.rationale: It manages whole files and doesn’t reorder their lines.

options.text: It sends every new log message to the administrator by email as soon as it appears.
options.rationale: That is not its purpose; it handles file size and age.

options.text: It renames old log files, for example to `syslog.1`, and starts new ones so logs don’t fill the disk.
options.rationale: Old copies may be compressed and are deleted after some time.

options.text: It turns the binary systemd journal into text files in `/var/log`.
options.rationale: The journal is read with `journalctl`, and logrotate works on files.

explanation: Log files grow without end, so a tool called logrotate regularly renames the current file (`syslog` becomes `syslog.1`), starts a fresh one, compresses old copies and deletes the oldest ones.

stem: Which TWO statements about `systemctl` are correct? (Choose TWO.)

options.text: `systemctl status` shows whether a service is running, on its `Active:` line.
options.rationale: The line reads, for example, `active (running)` or `failed`.

options.text: `systemctl stop` deletes the unit file, so the service can never be started again.
options.rationale: `stop` only ends the running service; the unit file stays.

options.text: `systemctl start` also enables the service for every following boot.
options.rationale: `start` and `enable` are separate actions.

options.text: `systemctl start` runs the service now but doesn’t make it start at boot.
options.rationale: `enable` is needed for that.

options.text: `systemctl status` restarts a service that has failed.
options.rationale: `status` only reports; `restart` changes the state.

explanation: `start`, `stop` and `status` act on the service as it is now: they start it, end it and report its state. Whether it starts at boot is decided by `enable` and `disable`.

stem: Mira wants the last 20 journal messages of the `ssh` service. Which TWO options does she combine with `journalctl`? (Choose TWO.)

options.rationale: It limits the output to that unit.
It would restrict the output to kernel messages.
It follows the journal and keeps waiting for new messages.
It selects messages of the current boot only and doesn’t pick a unit.
It shows only the last 20 lines.

explanation: `journalctl -u ssh -n 20` combines a unit filter and a line count. `-k` selects kernel messages, `-b` the current boot and `-f` follows new messages as they arrive.

stem: Which TWO files under `/proc` hold facts about the machine that can be read with `cat`? (Choose TWO.)

options.rationale: User accounts are in `/etc/passwd`.
No such file exists, and the machine name is in `/etc/hostname`.
It describes the processor.
Login records are kept elsewhere, such as in `/var/log/wtmp`.
It reports the memory.

explanation: `/proc` is a pseudo-filesystem that the kernel builds on the fly. `/proc/cpuinfo` describes the processor and `/proc/meminfo` the memory, and `/proc/uptime` and `/proc/version` give the uptime and the kernel version. The files take no space on disk.

stem: Which THREE of these are syslog priorities (severity levels)? (Choose THREE.)

options.rationale: It is a facility that says who sent the message.
It is a priority between `err` and `notice`.
It is a normal but significant condition.
It is a facility for the mail system.
It is a facility for background services.
It is the least serious priority.

explanation: Priorities say how serious a message is: `emerg`, `alert`, `crit`, `err`, `warning`, `notice`, `info`, `debug`. Facilities such as `auth`, `mail`, `kern` and `daemon` say who sent it.

stem: Which TWO statements about `free` are correct? (Choose TWO.)

options.text: `free` lists every process together with its memory use.
options.rationale: That is the job of `ps` and `top`.

options.text: The `swap` line shows the memory of the graphics card.
options.rationale: Swap is disk space the kernel uses as extra memory.

options.text: A `free` figure close to zero means the machine has crashed.
options.rationale: It usually just means the memory is used as cache.

options.text: `free -h` prints the sizes in human-readable units such as `Gi`.
options.rationale: `-h` stands for human-readable.

options.text: A small `free` figure is normal, because Linux uses spare RAM as a cache.
options.rationale: The `available` column is the better guide.

explanation: `free` summarises memory and swap. Linux fills spare RAM with cached disk data, so the `free` column is often small even on a healthy machine, and `available` tells what programs could still use.

stem: Which TWO files are typical text log files under `/var/log` on a Debian-based system? (Choose TWO.)

options.rationale: It is a configuration file that holds the machine’s name.
It is a live view of the processor and not a log.
It records package installations and removals.
It records logins and `sudo` use.
It is the kernel image, a binary file.

explanation: Services write text logs under `/var/log`: `dpkg.log` for package changes, `auth.log` for authentication, and `syslog` for general messages. Plain text tools work on them.

stem: Which TWO commands show messages from the kernel? (Choose TWO.)

options.rationale: It prints the kernel ring buffer.
It lists processes and doesn’t show kernel messages.
It shows memory use.
It shows the kernel messages that the journal collected.
It shows the state of one service.

explanation: Kernel messages are kept in the ring buffer, which `dmesg` prints. On systemd systems `journalctl -k` shows the same messages from the journal.

stem: Type the command, with its options, that prints a snapshot of every process in the full format, with the UID, PID and PPID columns.
explanation: `-e` (or `-A`) selects every process and `-f` chooses the full format. `ps aux` is the BSD-style way to list all processes.

stem: Type the command with the short option that shows the memory and swap use in human-readable sizes such as `Gi`.
explanation: `free -h` (long form `--human`) prints sizes as `Mi` or `Gi`, and `free -m` prints megabytes.

stem: Type the full command, without `sudo`, that shows the state of the service `buildd`, including its `Active:` line.
explanation: `systemctl status NAME` prints the unit’s state: the `Loaded:` and `Active:` lines, the main PID and the last few log lines. It needs no root rights.

stem: Type the full command that prints only the last 20 lines of the systemd journal.
explanation: `journalctl -n 20` (long form `--lines=20`) prints the newest 20 journal lines. Without it, `journalctl` prints the whole journal, starting with the oldest messages.

stem: Type the absolute path of the file that describes the processor of the machine, such as its model and number of cores.
explanation: `/proc/cpuinfo` is made up by the kernel when it is read. It holds one block per processor core.

stem: Ada wants to see the last two lines of the build daemon’s log. Complete the command with the path of the log file.
explanation: `tail -n 2` prints the last two lines of a file. The build daemon’s log is an ordinary text file under `/var/log`.

stem: Ada looks up the number of workers in the build daemon’s configuration file. What does this command print?

options.rationale: The configuration says four workers, not eight.
The settings file uses `=` and no colon.

options.text: # Settings for the Pixel Raiders build daemon
options.rationale: That comment line doesn’t contain the word `workers`.
The configuration file contains exactly one line with `workers`, and `grep` prints that line.

explanation: Configuration files under `/etc` are plain text. `grep` prints the lines that contain the word, here the setting `workers=4`.

stem: How many lines of the build log contain the word `ERROR` in capital letters? What does this command print?

options.rationale: The log does contain one ERROR line.
Only the linker failure is logged at the level ERROR. The lines about warnings and `0 errors` don’t match.
Only one line has the word in capitals.
That is the number of lines in the whole log.

explanation: `grep -c` counts the matching lines instead of printing them. Matching is case-sensitive, so `ERROR` doesn’t match the lowercase word `errors`.

stem: The last line of the build log looks like `Nov 26 22:08:55 build01 buildd[402]: …`. Type what this command prints.
explanation: `tail -n 1` takes the last line, and `cut -d" " -f6-` keeps everything from the sixth space-separated field on, which is the message after the program name and its PID.

stem: The kernel makes up `/proc/meminfo` when it is read. What does this command print?

options.rationale: `MemFree` is on the second line of the file.
The first line of the file starts with the label `MemTotal`, and `cut` keeps only the part before the colon.
There is no label called `Memory`.
The label is written `MemTotal`, in this exact form.

explanation: The first line of `/proc/meminfo` reports the total memory as `MemTotal: … kB`. `cut -d: -f1` keeps the part before the colon.

stem: `free` prints a header line, a line for the RAM and a line for the swap space. How many lines does this command print?

options.rationale: Besides the header and the RAM line, there is also a swap line.
`free` prints more than the header.
`free` doesn’t print separate lines for cache or buffers by default.
The header, the `Mem:` line and the `Swap:` line make three lines.

explanation: `free` shows a header, the `Mem:` line and the `Swap:` line. `wc -l` counts the lines. The figures change all the time, but the number of lines doesn’t.
